3.0.0.en: St. Paul had already taught them how their relationship with worldly authorities should be, and he asks his disciple Titus to remind them to submit to those in authority in the state and all its systems, and to obey the laws and statutes, because it is God who allowed the existence of these systems so that security and order may prevail, even if they persecute the Christians as the Romans did. This does not cancel obedience and submission to the state for God's sake; rather he asks them to be good citizens who strive to do not only what is asked of them but more than this, everything that benefits the state.

3.1.0.en: To speak evil of no man: the Apostle forbids condemnation, which is like stabs directed at others, and he means all the people around us.

3.1.1.en: To be no brawlers: if they differ with someone, they do not shun him and let their hearts fill with evil toward him, but keep their love for him and continue dealing and speaking with him, even if briefly.

3.1.2.en: Gentle: that is, showing love and tenderness to those who err and who wrong them.

3.1.3.en: Showing all meekness unto all men: with calm hearts they bear with others and even absorb all the agitation in them, so they spread peace around them.

3.1.4.en: The Apostle calls them not to condemn and quarrel, but to be adorned with longsuffering and calm in dealing with all people.

3.1.5.en: The more you are occupied with the love of God, the smaller material things and the world become in your sight, and you even love everyone and have compassion on them however much they err, and you incline to making peace and solving all the problems you meet, so that you remain attached to the love of God.

3.2.s.en: (2) Salvation through Baptism and its effects on our life

3.2.0.en: For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish: he reminds them of their state before the faith, how they did not know God, so they were foolish in not knowing the truth. And as they remember their weakness they are not annoyed by the faults of those around them but bear with them gently, as was mentioned in the previous verse.

3.2.1.en: Disobedient, deceived: they do not obey God and consequently walk in error, far from the truth. Serving divers lusts and pleasures: since they were far from God, it was easy for them to fall into evil desires such as adultery, the love of wine and the love of money.

3.2.2.en: Living in malice and envy: they were not content with defiling their senses and bodies, but their hearts became corrupt and filled with evil toward others.

3.2.3.en: Hateful: because of these evils they lost the love of others for them, in addition to the wrath of God. Hating one another: they too came to hate others because of their competition with them over material things and their fear and anxiety of everyone.

3.3.0.en: The Apostle declares our change in the New Testament from evil to good by the work of the grace of God and His tenderness toward us.

3.3.1.en: God our Savior: the Father is our Savior because He sent His beloved Son to redeem us, for the three hypostases shared in salvation: the Father sent His Son, the Son redeemed us on the Cross, and the Holy Spirit gives us this salvation in the Church.

3.4.0.en: Not by works of righteousness which we have done: good works are a natural result in the life of the believing children of God, but works alone without the grace of God do not give us salvation, since salvation was accomplished on the Cross and we receive it in the Holy Sacraments, the first of which is Baptism.

3.4.1.en: But according to His mercy He saved us: it is the grace of God that gave us salvation in Baptism, and this salvation is given to us in stages. The first is in Baptism, by the death of the nature inclined to evil within us and our birth with a new nature inclined to be like God; then this salvation is completed through our spiritual striving throughout our life and is perfected in eternity.

3.4.2.en: By the washing of regeneration: it is immersion in the water of Baptism, so we are washed and cleansed from all our sins: the ancestral sin which we inherited from Adam and Eve, and also our sins which we committed ourselves if we were adults when we were baptized.

3.4.3.en: And renewing of the Holy Ghost: it is the work of the Holy Spirit in us, by putting to death the old man, that is, the nature inclined to evil, when we are buried in the water of Baptism, and giving us a new nature inclined to good so that we may live by it with God.

3.5.0.en: The work of the Holy Spirit in us begins with the sacrament of Baptism and continues to pour out upon us generously in the Holy Sacraments, such as forgiveness in the sacrament of repentance and confession, and strength and spiritual nourishment in the sacrament of Communion, and likewise His work in us through all the spiritual practices: He encourages us to pray and reveals to us the depths of His love in the Holy Bible, and He continues to work in us through all the situations of our life, guiding us, directing us and supporting us. And this salvation which the Holy Spirit continues to give us is through the redemption which our Lord Jesus Christ accomplished on the Cross for our sake.

3.6.0.en: That being justified by His grace: the salvation we receive through the Holy Sacraments and the means of grace gives us righteousness, that is, a life of purity and an inclination to doing good.

3.6.1.en: We should be made heirs: we come to have a place in the heavenly Kingdom, which we receive as a grace from Christ the Savior, who died for us and gives us this inheritance.

3.6.2.en: According to the hope of eternal life: this Kingdom we hope for with patience in spiritual striving and steadfastness in the faith until we receive it after this life.

3.6.3.en: Remember the great grace you received in Baptism by the renewal of your nature, and so thank God at all times, especially when people praise you, and keep away from every evil and from what does not befit your new life, and advance on the way of the love of God. Remind yourself at the beginning of each day of this new nature so that you may enjoy the work of the Holy Spirit in you.

3.7.0.en: This is a faithful saying: he confirms the importance of the preceding words which he mentioned in this epistle. And these things I will that thou affirm constantly: he prepares for the importance of the principle which he will declare and the necessity of teaching it to the believers in the Church.

3.7.1.en: That they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works: relying on the work of grace in salvation does not mean being lax in good works, which are striving in worship, serving others and works of goodness. For these good works are evidence of the sincerity of faith and of submission to the work of grace, and without them man does not obtain salvation.

3.7.2.en: These things are good and profitable unto men: that is, the principle of caring for good works is what benefits the believers if they hold fast to it.

3.8.0.en: Foolish questions: argument and discussion that does not arrive at anything useful.

3.8.1.en: Genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law: some Christians of Jewish origin, who were the false teachers, boasted of their descent from Abraham and proclaimed the necessity of holding to circumcision and the works of the Law to obtain salvation, and in their insistence on this teaching they create parties and quarrels within the Church.

3.8.2.en: Avoid them; for they are unprofitable and vain: he charges his disciple Titus and all the believers to avoid discussions with the false teachers and their followers, because this talk stirs up tension and benefits nothing.

3.9.0.en: A man that is an heretick: that is, the false teacher who proclaims teachings foreign to the Church, such as the necessity of circumcision and the works of the Law.

3.9.1.en: After the first and second admonition: Bishop Titus must rebuke him and warn him more than once to turn back from this strange teaching, that is, give him a chance to repent.

3.9.2.en: Reject: do not argue with him and waste your time, because he is insistent on his sin.

3.10.0.en: This heretic is insistent on deviating from the truth and the teachings of the Church, and by this he has condemned himself as a heretic, separated from the Church and not a member of it, and nothing awaits him but destruction.

3.10.1.en: How good it is for you to review your speech with others: is it beneficial for your life and theirs, or is it futile and harms you and them?

3.10.2.en: Take care to speak what is beneficial, and if you are in a place filled with talk that does not glorify God, either try to change the talk to a useful subject or withdraw.

3.11.0.en: When I shall send unto thee: Paul will send one of his disciples to Titus in Crete to take his place in leading the Church there, so that Titus can travel to Paul to meet him. Artemas: one of Paul's disciples, mentioned only in this place, and his name is derived from the goddess Artemis, so he is a Christian of Gentile origin.

3.11.1.en: Tychicus: one of Paul's disciples, whose name is of Greek origin and means “fortunate,” and he is from Asia Minor (Acts 20:4). He was with Paul in his first imprisonment in Rome, and Paul sent him with epistles to Ephesus (Eph 6:21, 22) and Colossae (Col 4:7, 8), and he was also with Paul in his second imprisonment in Rome before his martyrdom, and Paul sent him to Ephesus (2 Tim 4:12). Paul was going to send one of these two disciples to Titus in Crete to lead the Church in his place so that he could leave Crete and go to meet Paul. Nicopolis: a city in northern Greece near Illyricum and Dalmatia.

3.11.2.en: Be diligent to come ... for I have determined there to winter: he asks him to come quickly and meet him at Nicopolis, because winter had drawn near, and Paul was then in Ephesus or near Nicopolis, and so he would reach it quickly.

3.12.0.en: Zenas the lawyer: one of Paul's disciples, whose name is derived from the god Zeus; he is of Gentile origin but a student of the Law and also of the spiritual canons.

3.12.1.en: Apollos: one of Paul's companions, whose name is derived from the god Apollo; he is of Gentile origin and was renowned for eloquence and preaching (Acts 18:24, 25). Bring ... diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them: these two servants were helping Titus in the service of the Church of Crete, and Paul asked Titus to provide for their material needs for the journey so that they could continue preaching in other places, so that they would lack nothing in their new ministry and would not burden anyone.

3.13.0.en: Ours also: the servants and the believers in the Church.

3.13.1.en: St. Paul takes this opportunity to call all the servants and believers to care for the service of others, especially providing the necessities of life for the servants and all those in need, for these works of love are fruits of the Holy Spirit and virtues with which the believers must be adorned.

3.14.0.en: All that are with me salute thee: he means Paul's disciples who are with him in Ephesus and whom Titus knows, so they send greetings to him.

3.14.1.en: Greet them that love us in the faith: all the believers in the Church of Crete.

3.14.2.en: The Apostle concludes the epistle by sending his greeting and the greeting of the servants accompanying him to Titus and all the believers in Crete, hoping for them the constant work of the grace of Christ in them.

3.14.3.en: May you feel the needs of those around you and try to help them if they ask, or even if they do not ask you. For just as God feels for you and provides for your needs, care for those around you, so that your heart is filled with love and the mercies of God overflow upon you.
